title: 5-Fluorouracil in primary, impending recurrent and recurrent pterygium: Systematic review of the efficacy and safety of a surgical adjuvant and intralesional antimetabolite
condition_or_topic: Use of 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) in primary, impending recurrent, and recurrent pterygium
clinical_background: Pterygium is associated with ultraviolet exposure and involves an abnormal, active wound-healing process. Recurrence, which most often arises within the first 12 months after surgery, involves fibrovascular growth and inflammation; there is no agreed definition of recurrence. Medical treatments may be used when recurrence becomes apparent. 5-FU has been applied topically or by injection to prevent recurrence after surgery and, more recently, by intralesional subconjunctival injection to halt progression. Its cytotoxicity raises concern about short- and long-term complications. The authors identified no previous review devoted exclusively to its use, efficacy, and safety in pterygium.
objectives: Summarize clinical evidence on the efficacy and safety of 5-FU for pterygium management.
Examine recurrence outcomes when 5-FU is used as a surgical adjuvant or as an intralesional subconjunctival injection.
Describe complications associated with 5-FU and, on the basis of the reviewed evidence, provide recommendations about its current and future roles in pterygium management.
clinical_question: In people with primary, impending recurrent, or recurrent pterygium (P), how does topical or intralesional subconjunctival 5-FU, used with surgery or as a treatment without surgery (I), compare with other treatments or control groups where available (C) in terms of recurrence or arrest of progression and complications (O)?
study_design: Systematic review of clinical studies. Searches covered Ovid Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, Global Health, and Web of Science Core Collection from database inception through July 2022, without language restrictions at the search stage. Reference lists were also searched. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted study data; disagreements were settled by discussion and consensus with a third reviewer.

population.description: Human participants with primary, impending recurrent, or recurrent pterygium in clinical studies reporting recurrence outcomes after 5-FU use.
inclusion_criteria: Clinical studies involving humans with primary, impending recurrent, or recurrent pterygium that reported recurrence outcomes after 5-FU use.
Any study design and any 5-FU dose were eligible, whether treatment was topical or delivered by intralesional subconjunctival injection, with or without surgery.
exclusion_criteria: Studies for which an English full-text manuscript could not be obtained.
Review articles, conference proceedings and abstracts, editorials, expert opinions, and grey literature.
Less complete duplicate reports from institutions that subsequently reported more patients or longer follow-up.

interventions: Topical 5-FU used as a surgical adjuvant to prevent pterygium recurrence.
Preoperative or intraoperative intralesional subconjunctival 5-FU injections used as surgical adjuvants.
Postoperative intralesional subconjunctival 5-FU injections for impending recurrent pterygium or recurrent pterygium with corneal involvement.
Intralesional subconjunctival 5-FU injections as treatment for primary or recurrent pterygium without surgery.
comparators: Triamcinolone injection or a control group for impending recurrence.
5-FU injection with cyclosporine A compared with 5-FU injection without cyclosporine A.

primary: Pterygium recurrence rate, including progression after treatment where assessed.
secondary: Cosmetic appearance of the pterygium where assessed.

interpretation: The reviewed evidence does not convincingly support preoperative or intraoperative 5-FU as an adjunct to prevent pterygium recurrence. Reported recurrence rates were 11.4–60% with bare scleral surgery, 3.5–35.8% with conjunctival rotational flaps, 3.7–9.6% with conjunctival autografts, and 14–35.8% with preoperative or intraoperative injections. By contrast, postoperative intralesional injections showed more promising results in arresting impending recurrence and true recurrence, with reported success rates of 87.2–100% and 75–100%, respectively. Injections without surgery arrested progression in 81.3–96% of primary and recurrent pterygia. These findings must be weighed against potential corneal, scleral, and graft-related toxicity and the lack of long-term safety evidence.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors note that bare scleral surgery itself has unacceptably high recurrence rates, while newer reconstructive techniques achieve lower rates without antimetabolite exposure. In individual cited comparisons, Kareem et al. found MMC more effective than 5-FU as an adjunct to bare scleral surgery (8% vs. 18%, odds ratio 5.4 vs. 1.4, p = 0.04), whereas Altay et al. found no significant difference (12.5% vs. 27.6%, p = 0.13). Bekibele et al. reported that conjunctival autografting alone was noninferior to bare scleral surgery with 5-FU (12.1% vs. 11.4% recurrence, p > 0.05). For impending recurrence, Prabhasawat et al. found intralesional 5-FU more successful than triamcinolone or topical steroids alone (87.2% vs. 71.4% vs. 48.6%); Zhang et al. found conbercept more effective than 5-FU. Evidence cited for cyclosporine suggests benefit in several surgical settings, whereas findings for anti-VEGF agents remain inconclusive overall.
clinical_implications: The comparatively poor recurrence outcomes of perioperative 5-FU limit its clinical value as a surgical adjunct, including where resources are scarce.

Intralesional 5-FU may arrest fibrovascular progression and improve appearance in selected primary or recurrent pterygia; some patients may choose not to undergo surgery if a less invasive treatment improves overall cosmetic appearance.
Recognizing impending recurrence before fibrovascular tissue extends onto the cornea and treating it promptly is likely to improve the chance of success.

5-FU toxicity increases with greater dose or repeated exposure. Reported complications range from temporary findings to potentially sight-threatening corneal injury, scleral thinning, and graft problems.
Although complications reported with injections appear less frequent than those reported with topical application, a direct comparison did not demonstrate a significant reduction in complications.
The possibility of delayed toxicity remains relevant because 5-FU may retain antimitotic effects after treatment stops; existing follow-up cannot establish its long-term safety.
practice_implications: The authors recommend against 5-FU as an adjunct to pterygium surgery, even in resource-limited settings, because of its inferior efficacy.

For intralesional treatment, assess patients individually rather than applying a fixed injection count; the authors note that a clinical effect typically requires two to four injections, although substantially more have been used.
When 5-FU is used, select patients carefully, administer it cautiously, and maintain vigilant long-term monitoring, particularly after repeated exposure.
Discuss the potential benefits, risks, and short- and long-term complications of 5-FU with the patient.
The authors caution against 5-FU in patients with current or previous intrinsic corneal disorders and suggest that avoiding it may also be preferable in those with a family history of pterygium.
Patients receiving injections need to adhere to follow-up visits and the injection regimen.
Clinicians using corticosteroids for impending recurrence should monitor for steroid-induced ocular hypertension.
limitations: Long-term efficacy and safety evidence for intralesional 5-FU in pterygium is insufficient: many published studies followed patients for no longer than six months, and very few exceeded 24 months. Delayed adverse effects may therefore have been missed.
The three-month follow-up in the studies by Silva et al. and Schellini et al. may have missed additional recurrences, which usually arise within the first 12 postoperative months.
Reported recurrence rates may be affected by pterygium type and size, genetic predisposition, surgical technique, geographical location, and surgeon experience.
Published injection regimens differ substantially in total dose and number of administrations, leaving the optimal regimen undetermined.
strengths: The authors present the review as a comprehensive assessment focused specifically on the application, efficacy, and safety of 5-FU across primary, impending recurrent, and recurrent pterygium.
open_questions: What dose, injection frequency, and treatment duration provide the best balance of efficacy and safety for intralesional 5-FU?
How effective and safe are intralesional 5-FU injections over longer follow-up, including after repeated exposure?
Do intralesional injections change how often patients elect surgical excision?
What are the optimal dose, frequency, duration, and administration method of anti-VEGF treatment for pterygium?
future_directions: Conduct further clinical studies of intralesional 5-FU with extended follow-up to assess efficacy, delayed complications, and the optimal dose, frequency, and duration.
Report whether injection treatment affects patients’ decisions to undergo surgical excision, including its potential cost-benefit implications.
Consider using recently published cosmetic grading systems to assess appearance in future injection studies.

main_conclusion: The authors do not recommend 5-FU as an adjunct to pterygium surgery because its prevention of recurrence is insufficient and it carries corneal, scleral and graft-related risks. Intralesional injections after surgery or without surgery appear more promising for limiting progression, but their optimal regimen and long-term safety require further study; if used, 5-FU calls for careful patient selection and vigilant long-term monitoring.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review assessed the efficacy and safety of 5-FU for primary, impending recurrent and recurrent pterygium. Searches of six databases and reference lists identified 34 eligible clinical studies reporting recurrence outcomes. The authors examined topical and injected 5-FU as a surgical adjunct, postoperative intralesional injections, and injections used without surgery.

For intraoperative topical 5-FU, reported recurrence was 11.4–60% with BST, 3.5–35.8% with conjunctival flaps and 3.7–9.6% with conjunctival autografts. Results for preoperative and intraoperative injections were also insufficient to persuade the authors to recommend 5-FU for prevention of surgical recurrence. By contrast, postoperative injections arrested progression in 87.2–100% of impending recurrences and 75–100% of true recurrences; injection-only treatment arrested progression in 81.3–96% of primary and recurrent pterygia.

The authors emphasize that adverse effects can involve corneal toxicity, scleral thinning and graft complications, and may be severe or threaten sight. Although complications reported with injections were generally transient in the short term, follow-up in many studies was brief. The optimal injection dose, frequency and duration, together with long-term efficacy and safety, remain unresolved. Where 5-FU injections are used, the authors advise caution, discussion of risks and benefits, careful selection of patients and vigilant long-term monitoring.

The complication summary reports, for injections, corneal abrasion 35.4%, persistent corneal epithelial defect 6.25%, graft hyperemia 100%, elevated intraocular pressure 17.9%, subconjunctival hemorrhage 16.7–100%, scleral dellen or thinning 2%, superficial punctate keratopathy 1.5–6.25%, and wound or graft dehiscence 32.1%. The review links 5-FU to potential severe corneal complications, including keratitis, ulceration, melting, and perforation; it emphasizes that long-term safety in pterygium has not been established.

subgroup_analyses: For topical 5-FU used as a surgical adjuvant, published recurrence ranges differed by technique: BST 11.4–60%, CTF 3.5–35.8%, and CAG 3.7–9.6%. These were ranges across studies rather than a formal pooled subgroup analysis.

For Shiratori et al.'s single preoperative injection given 30 days before surgery, recurrence was 52.9% in primary and 75% in recurrent pterygium; when given 10 days before surgery, recurrence was 27.3% in primary and 47.1% in recurrent pterygium.
For postoperative 5-FU injections, published success ranges were 87.2–100% in impending conjunctival recurrence and 75–100% in true corneal recurrence.
For Malik et al.'s injections without surgery, reported improvement was 85.2% for primary and 81.3% for recurrent pterygium.
Shah et al. reported comparable effectiveness of nonsurgical 5-FU injections in primary and recurrent pterygium without giving separate success rates.
secondary_results: Garcia Tirado et al. reported improved cosmesis in 60% after injections for postoperative recurrence, while astigmatism showed no change from baseline.

Shah et al. reported improvement in clinical grade in 87.1% after nonsurgical injections (p < 0.001). Before treatment, the grading counts were atrophic n = 0, intermediate n = 46, and fleshy n = 55; after 3 injections they were atrophic n = 42, intermediate n = 50, and fleshy n = 9.
Ghoz et al. reported improved cosmesis in 62.5% with combined 5-FU and Avastin injections. Astigmatism decreased in 22%, was unchanged in 11%, and increased in 67% from baseline.
Malik et al. reported improvement in clinical appearance in 100% after nonsurgical 5-FU injections and a nonsignificant reduction in astigmatism.

The review reports that 25.7% of 101 patients treated solely with 5-FU injections and 53% of 15 patients in another cited cohort elected surgical excision; it does not establish that injections caused those decisions.

In cited laboratory studies, a single 5-min exposure to 5-FU 25 mg/ml reduced human Tenon's capsule fibroblasts by 50%; continuous exposure to 1 mg/ml for greater than three days resulted in death of the entire fibroblast population over a 30-day period. Other cited experiments reported a 50% reduction in SV40-immortalized human corneal epithelial cells by 24 h and complete cell death by 72 h with 5-FU 5 mg/ml, and death of >50% of human limbal stem cells at 160 μM. These are laboratory findings, not clinical recurrence outcomes.

Among cited studies of alternative treatments, topical cyclosporine versus placebo was associated with recurrence rates of 22% vs. 44% and 20.6% vs. 45.5% after BST, 23% vs. 46% after conjunctival rotational flaps, and 7.5% vs. 17.5% after CAG. The review also describes a separate BST comparison of 22.2% vs. 44.4%.

In a cited trial by Prabhasawat et al. involving impending recurrence, intralesional 5-FU had a success rate of 87.2%, Triamcinolone injection 71.4%, and the control group receiving topical steroids alone 48.6%.

The review describes anti-VEGF efficacy as inconclusive across cited studies. For impending recurrence, a cited study reported corneal recurrence in 78% after a single bevacizumab injection, whereas another reported 95.7% success at 12 months after one to three injections. A cited trial by Zhang et al. reported 100% success with Conbercept versus 87.5% with 5-FU.

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Pterygium is associated with ultraviolet exposure and abnormal, active wound healing. Recurrence is distressing for patients and surgeons, prompting investigation of surgical adjuncts. This systematic review evaluates the efficacy and safety of 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) for primary, impending recurrent and recurrent pterygium. Searches of six databases identified 34 clinical studies reporting recurrence outcomes. Experimental studies found cytostatic and cytotoxic effects that varied with dose and exposure duration. Although 5-FU is relatively inexpensive, accessible and straightforward to administer, recurrence after intraoperative topical use was 11.4–60% with bare sclera surgery, 3.5–35.8% with conjunctival rotational flaps and 3.7–9.6% with conjunctival autografts; preoperative and intraoperative injections yielded recurrence of 14–35.8%. Because surgical-adjuvant efficacy is inadequate, the authors do not recommend that use. Postoperative intralesional injections appeared more promising: reported success was 87.2–100% for impending recurrence and 75–100% for true recurrence. Without surgery, injections arrested progression in 81.3–96% of primary and recurrent pterygia. The review also considers corticosteroids, cyclosporine and anti-VEGF agents. Increasing 5-FU exposure increases the risk of complications, which can be reversible or sight-threatening; scleral thinning, corneal toxicity and graft complications are particular concerns. Longer studies are needed to establish injection dose, frequency, duration and long-term safety. If used, 5-FU calls for selected patients, caution and vigilant long-term monitoring.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Pterygium is a conspicuous ultraviolet-associated ocular disorder involving centripetal expansion of altered limbal epithelial cells. Squamous metaplasia with goblet-cell hyperplasia develops alongside proliferating stromal fibroblasts, new vessels, inflammation and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Reactivation of this wound-healing process by surgery may explain recurrence better than the older degenerative account involving Bowman’s layer degradation and elastosis. Epidemiological evidence and associations with cataract, climatic droplet keratopathy, photo-aged skin, squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma, melanoma and inherited DNA-repair disease support a role for chronic ultraviolet exposure. Prior studies also implicate peripheral-light focusing, fixation, ocular dominance and eye closure in sunlight, corneal curvature, anterior-chamber depth and handedness in pterygium location or laterality. Management seeks to restore ocular-surface anatomy, function and appearance while relieving symptoms; the authors have advocated excision with a limbal-conjunctival autograft as a reconstructive standard. Recurrence is most likely during the first 12 months after surgery and involves fibrovascular invasion and inflammation. Conjunctival recurrence and corneal recurrence after limbal breach have been described, but no consensus definition exists. Once recurrence is apparent, medical treatment is initially used to lessen or stop progression. Options mentioned include corticosteroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, cyclosporine, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) and antimetabolites. 5-Fluourouracil (5-FU) has been applied topically or by injection as a surgical adjunct; intralesional subconjunctival injections have also attracted interest for primary, impending recurrent and recurrent disease. Its cytotoxicity raises concern about immediate and delayed harms. The authors knew of no prior review devoted exclusively to its application, effectiveness and safety in pterygium. They therefore set out to synthesize clinical recurrence outcomes, complications and possible present and future roles.

document_sections.heading: 2. Method of literature search
document_sections.content: The review used a literature search, eligibility assessment and independent data extraction to examine clinical recurrence outcomes and complications associated with 5-FU in pterygium.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Search strategy and study selection
document_sections.content: Ovid Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, Global Health and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception through July 2022 without search-language restrictions. The keyword strategy combined (pterygium OR pterygia) with (5-fluorouracil OR fluorouracil OR 5-FU OR antimetabolite); reference lists of reviews and potentially relevant studies provided additional records. BWHL and AS screened titles and abstracts independently. A full text was assessed when either considered it potentially eligible, and inclusion disagreements were settled through discussion and consensus with MTC.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Eligibility criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible human studies examined primary, impending recurrent or recurrent pterygium treated with 5-FU and reported recurrence outcomes. Any study design, dose and topical or intralesional subconjunctival route could qualify, whether treatment occurred without surgery or before, during or after it. The prespecified clinical roles were prevention of surgical recurrence, postoperative treatment of impending conjunctival or established corneal recurrence, and stand-alone treatment of primary or recurrent disease. Studies without an obtainable English full-text manuscript were omitted. Reviews, conference proceedings and abstracts, editorials, expert opinions and grey literature were excluded. For overlapping institutional reports with increasing enrollment or follow-up, only the most complete report was retained.

document_sections.heading: 2.3. Data extraction
document_sections.content: BWHL and AS independently extracted information from articles, tables and figures, resolving discrepancies by discussion and consensus with MTC. Recurrence and complications were primary outcomes. Recorded study characteristics included authors, year, country, design, pterygium category and count, surgery, 5-FU dose and delivery, controls, sample size, follow-up and the definition of recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 2.4. Results of systematic review
document_sections.content: Searching six databases and reference lists yielded 1135 distinct records. Title and abstract screening excluded 1072; full texts of the remaining 62 were assessed, and 34 studies satisfied eligibility criteria. Study selection was depicted in a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses flowchart. Surgical-adjuvant use appeared in 20 studies: 16 examined topical application and 4 examined injections. Postoperative intralesional injections were covered by 4 reports on impending recurrence and 6 on true recurrence; another 4 reports assessed injections as stand-alone treatment for primary or recurrent pterygium. The clinical-study tables present interventions, populations, follow-up, recurrence or success definitions and outcomes, and reported complications.

document_sections.heading: 3. 5-Fluorouracil
document_sections.content: Duschinsky et al. first synthesized 5-FU in 1957. Ophthalmic use began in 1982; the earliest published pterygium applications identified were those of Radda and Grasl in 1989 and Carlentini et al. in 1991. A 2019 survey of 199 cornea specialists found routine 5-FU use in 0% for primary pterygium and 1.7% for early recurrence. A 2013 American Academy of Ophthalmology assessment of surgical adjuncts did not address its role or safety. Nevertheless, use persists internationally, particularly where health resources or surgical expertise are limited, possibly because the drug is relatively inexpensive, readily available, simple to administer and requires no refrigeration.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Ocular pharmacology and pharmacokinetics
document_sections.content: 5-FU is a pyrimidine analogue described as suppressing DNA replication through competitive thymidylate-synthase inhibition and thymidine incorporation into DNA; its activity is selective for the synthesis phase of the cell cycle. Antimetabolite effects depend on concentration and exposure duration, and higher concentrations also interfere with RNA synthesis and the actin cytoskeleton. Ocular-surface exposure promotes apoptosis in Tenon’s capsule fibroblasts and inhibits proliferation of conjunctival fibroblasts and corneal epithelial cells. Other studies reported no effect on fibroblast attachment, migration or collagen secretion, or on vascular endothelial growth factor expression.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Ocular in vitro and in vivo studies
document_sections.content: Experimental studies demonstrate cytostatic or cytotoxic effects on ocular cells, particularly after repeated or prolonged exposure. Khaw et al. found that one intraoperative 5-min exposure to 5-FU (25 mg/ml) reduced human Tenon’s capsule fibroblasts by 50%; continuous exposure to 1 mg/ml for greater than three days killed the entire fibroblast population over a 30-day period. Other investigations found significantly delayed rabbit corneal epithelial healing and several days of impaired subconjunctival and scleral fibroblast recovery. In a bovine in-vitro system, Nuyts et al. observed corneal endothelial toxicity after 30 min at 50 mg/ml. Huhtala et al. reported a 50% decline in cultured SV40-immortalized human corneal epithelial cells by 24 h at 5 mg/ml, followed by complete cell death by 72 h. Midena et al. described exposure-time-dependent toxicity in human corneal epithelial cells with 1% 5-FU (10 mg/ml). Concentrations of 0.5, 1, and 5 mg/ml also reduced corneal epithelial stem-cell viability, disrupted mitochondrial transmembrane potential and induced apoptosis according to exposure time and dose. Gallo et al. found that 160 μM killed >50% of human limbal stem cells. Together, these findings raise concern about substantial corneal-cell toxicity and possible long-term harm.

document_sections.heading: 4. Efficacy of 5-fluorouracil as a surgical adjuvant in preventing pterygium recurrence
document_sections.content: The review evaluates topical and injected 5-FU given around pterygium surgery. Its clinical-study table summarizes surgical approaches, doses, recurrence outcomes and complications.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Topical application in bare scleral technique
document_sections.content: Across published studies of primary and recurrent pterygium, intraoperative topical 5-FU with bare scleral surgery was followed by recurrence of 11.4 to 60%. Treatment generally involved placing a solution-soaked sponge over exposed sclera, sometimes including adjacent conjunctiva and Tenon’s space; most studies then rinsed with balanced salt solution. Concentrations ranged from 10 to 50 mg/ml and application lasted 1–5 min. Maldonado et al.’s prospective randomized, double-masked placebo-controlled trial found recurrence of 60% with 5-FU (10 mg/ml, 5 min) versus 35% with placebo (p = 0.11); in two bilateral cases, only treated eyes recurred. Those investigators considered that concentration inadequate. By contrast, Hassan et al.’s 2019 prospective series using 5 mg/ml for 5 min reported 12.8% recurrence after mean follow-up of 43 months. Majeed et al. found 32.5% recurrence with 25 mg/ml for 5 min versus 40% with bare scleral surgery alone. Two larger series of 125 and 75 primary cases treated at 25 mg/mL for 5 min reported 35.8% and 33.3% recurrence; smaller studies at that regimen reported 25.9% and 27.6%. Although adjuvant 5-FU lowered recurrence relative to bare scleral surgery alone in some studies, bare scleral surgery itself is regarded as having unacceptable recurrence. Bekibele et al. reported 25.9% recurrence with 5-FU versus 22.5% with β-irradiation as bare-sclera adjuncts. Akarsu et al. observed 25% recurrence after 25 mg/ml for 3 min, but used a conjunctival transpositional flap, which is considered less recurrence-prone than bare sclera. With 50 mg/mL for 3 to 5 min and bare sclera, reported recurrence declined to around 11 to 20%, although another study found 52%. Bekibele et al. found conjunctival autografting alone noninferior to bare scleral surgery plus 5-FU (50 mg/ml, 5 min): recurrence was 12.1% vs. 11.4% (p > 0.05). In comparisons with MMC, 5-FU was generally less effective. Kareem et al. reported 18% recurrence with 5-FU (50 mg/ml, 5 min) versus 34% in fellow placebo eyes (p = 0.03), while MMC (0.05%, 3 min) performed statistically better than 5-FU (8% vs. 18%, odds ratio 5.4 vs. 1.4, p = 0.04). Altay et al. found no statistically significant difference between 5-FU (25 mg/ml, 5 min) and MMC (0.02%, 5 min): 27.6% vs. 12.5% (p = 0.13). A separate cited trial reported that topical cyclosporine (0.05%) reduced recurrence after bare scleral surgery from 44.4% to 22.2% and was described as safer than antimetabolites.

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Topical application in conjunctival rotational flap and conjunctival autograft
document_sections.content: With a conjunctival transpositional flap, reported recurrence after topical 5-FU ranged from 3.5 to 35.8%; with conjunctival autografting it ranged from 3.7 to 9.6%. Silva et al. randomized 120 patients with bilateral primary disease to flap surgery with or without intraoperative 5-FU (25 mg/ml, 5 min), reporting a decline in recurrence from 25.5% to 5.8% with the drug. Schellini et al. reported 3.5% recurrence after the same 5-FU regimen with flap surgery for primary and recurrent disease. Both studies followed patients for only three months, potentially missing recurrence during the first 12 postoperative months. Two Bekibele et al. studies with follow-up exceeding 12 months found 3.7% and 8.7% recurrence using autografting and 5-FU (50 mg/ml, 5 min). A comparison favored 5-FU over MMC with autografting (8.7% vs. 11.8%). Another found similar effectiveness for 5-FU and one subconjunctival bevacizumab injection (0.05 ml of 0.5 mg): 3.7% vs. 3.9%. Kuldeep et al. reported recurrence of 7.7% and 8.3% for 10 and 20 mg/ml applied for 2 min, respectively; the review describes retained effects at lower doses.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Preoperative and intraoperative intralesional subconjunctival injections as a surgical adjuvant
document_sections.content: Only one eligible study investigated preoperative injections. In Shiratori et al.’s prospective series, 53 patients undergoing conjunctival transpositional-flap surgery received one 5 mg injection at 30 or 10 days before surgery; at 60 days, recurrence was 60% and 39.3%, respectively. The review considers one preoperative injection insufficient to prevent recurrence. Single intraoperative injections also showed limited efficacy, with recurrence of 14 to 35.8%. Meneghim et al. reported 29% recurrence after one 5 mg injection with flap surgery; adding cyclosporine (0.05%) for 10 days before and after surgery did not help and yielded 40% recurrence. Valezi et al. combined one 5 mg injection, topical intraoperative 5-FU (25 mg/ml, 5 min) and flap surgery in 125 patients, finding 35.8% recurrence. Ibrahim and Nada compared one 25 mg intraoperative injection with topical 5-FU (50 mg/ml, 5 min) during bare scleral surgery. Recurrence was 14% versus 20% (p > 0.05), respectively, over mean follow-up of 7.3 months. Their injections covered bare sclera, conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule. They proposed that their higher injected dose (25 mg vs. 5 mg) and broader injection area explained lower recurrence relative to Valezi et al.

document_sections.heading: 5. Recommendations for 5-fluorouracil as a surgical adjuvant in preventing pterygium recurrence
document_sections.content: The authors find no convincing evidence supporting preoperative or intraoperative 5-FU to prevent recurrence and recommend against its use as a surgical adjuvant, including where resources or surgical expertise are limited, because efficacy is inferior. They note that recurrence can vary with pterygium type and size, genetic predisposition, technique, geography and surgeon skill. Surveys and the scarcity of recent large studies indicate infrequent adjuvant use, although affordability and availability may sustain use in resource-limited settings. Evolving reconstructive techniques achieve very low recurrence without many antimetabolite risks, further questioning the drug’s adjunctive role. These operations can be lengthy and technically difficult; recurrence is higher among trainees and less experienced surgeons. Teaching models support acquisition of surgical and suturing skills. Femtosecond lasers might help less experienced surgeons create suitable conjunctival flaps, but have the same resource-setting limitation.

document_sections.heading: 6. Efficacy of intralesional subconjunctival injections of 5fluorouracil
document_sections.content: Postoperative 5-FU injections used to halt progression showed reported success of 87.2 to 100% for impending recurrence and 75 to 100% for true recurrence. When injections were the only treatment, success in arresting primary or recurrent pterygium ranged from 81.3 to 96%. The clinical-study table also reports dosing, follow-up, definitions of success, appearance-related outcomes and complications.

document_sections.heading: 6.1. Postoperative intralesional subconjunctival injections for impending recurrent pterygium (conjunctival recurrence)
document_sections.content: Impending conjunctival recurrence means localized fibrovascular tissue reappears at the excision site after initial postoperative redness and swelling subside. It features prominent, tortuous injected vessels and conjunctival thickening without corneal extension. Prabhasawat et al.’s 2006 prospective unmasked randomized trial compared 5-FU injections, triamcinolone and placebo after various operations. Its grading defined Grade I as a normal operative-site appearance; Grade II as fine episcleral vessels extending to the limbus without fibrous tissue; Grade III as fibrovascular tissue reaching the limbus without corneal invasion, indicating conjunctival recurrence; and Grade IV as fibrovascular invasion of the cornea. Two weekly 5-FU injections (5 mg) significantly outperformed placebo for preventing progression (87.2% vs. 48.6% success, p = 0.001) and improved the operative-site appearance. Kaplan-Meier analysis at one year also found a significantly longer recurrence-free period (p = 0.005). Zhang et al.’s 2020 randomized, double-blinded prospective controlled trial used the same grading and reported that three 5 mg injections at postoperative days 5, 14, and 28 arrested Grade II/III conjunctival recurrence and prevented corneal extension in 87.5% at six months. In Said et al.’s 2013 retrospective study of 15 impending recurrences, weekly injections of 2.5 to 5 mg continued until clinical effect; the majority required three. Appearance improved in 93.3%, with reduced vascularity and thickening and halted progression. Those investigators tailored injection count to clinical response and suggested that prompt treatment on detecting impending recurrence was critical.

document_sections.heading: 6.2. Postoperative intralesional subconjunctival injections for true recurrent pterygium (corneal recurrence)
document_sections.content: True corneal recurrence denotes fibrovascular growth beyond the limbus onto the cornea. Pikkel et al.’s 2001 pilot study treated six eyes with 0.5 to 1.5 mm corneal extension after bare scleral surgery and arrested progression in 83.3%. Total 5-FU dose ranged from 1 to 3 mg, injections numbered 2 to 4 and occurred an average 9.8 days apart; no additional growth was seen over 12 months of follow-up. One 1.5 mm recurrence nevertheless advanced to more than 2 mm after two injections; its patient attended follow-up three weeks late, which the investigators used to emphasize regimen adherence. Akarsu et al. treated four recurrences extending 1 to 2 mm after flap surgery with weekly 5 mg injections, up to four, and saw growth arrest with developing atrophy in 75%. The optimal injection number and dose remain unknown. Garcia Tirado et al. administered 10 weekly injections totaling 50 mg to 15 patients, 14 with corneal invasion (1.6 ± 0.8 mm, range 0 to 3 mm), and reported 100% progression arrest. Pherwani et al. described one 2.5 mm recurrence after amniotic membrane grafting that progressed despite three cycles of topical MMC (0.02%) four times a day for seven days, then stopped after 10 intralesional 5 mg injections given every one to two weeks over five months. Ul Haq et al. and Sabater-Cruz et al. reported arrest after as little as one 2 to 2.5 mg injection. Published regimens vary widely; two to four injections may generally suffice, although eight, ten or fourteen injections totaling 40 to 70 mg have been used. Some investigators favor adapting treatment to clinical response rather than imposing a fixed injection count that may underserve patients needing more drug.

document_sections.heading: 6.3. Intralesional subconjunctival injections as a sole treatment modality for primary and recurrent pterygium (no surgery)
document_sections.content: Reports of injection-only treatment describe progression-arrest success of 81.3 to 96%. Shah et al.’s 2021 study gave three weekly 5 mg injections to 101 patients described as 54 primary and 47 recurrent, without other topical medication. Initial grades were 1 (atrophic, n = 0), 2 (intermediate, n = 46) and 3 (fleshy, n = 55). After treatment, 87.1% improved by ≥ 1 grade (atrophic, n = 42; intermediate, n = 50; fleshy, n = 9; p < 0.001), with comparable efficacy in primary and recurrent disease. At six months, 13 remained unchanged and four progressed, yielding 96% success. Malik et al. gave 5 mg weekly for four weeks and reported improvement in fibrovascular growth and fleshy appearance in 85.2% of primary and 81.3% of recurrent cases; follow-up lasted only one month. Ghoz et al. reported synergistic effects from 2.5 mg intralesional 5-FU plus 2.5 to 5 mg bevacizumab every two weeks, up to five injections: progression stopped, atrophy developed and vascularity decreased in their cohort of 14 primary cases (100% success). Studies also assessed appearance, astigmatism and cytology. As surgical recurrence declines, appearance and patient satisfaction have become increasingly important. Among patients treated with injections alone, 25.7% of 101 patients and 53% of 15 patients chose surgical excision. Improved appearance from less invasive treatment may lead some patients to forgo surgery. Avoiding an operation may reduce scarring, operative risk, postoperative complications and use of limited donor tissue; repeated operations may themselves increase recurrence. Future investigations should report whether injections affect patients’ decisions about excision, potentially informing cost-benefit assessment, and could use recently published cosmetic grading systems.

document_sections.heading: 7. Recommendations for 5-fluorouracil as a postoperative intralesional subconjunctival injection and sole treatment modality for primary, impending recurrent, and recurrent pterygia
document_sections.content: The authors consider injection results promising for limiting progression and improving appearance in postoperative impending or established recurrence, and for treating primary or recurrent disease without surgery. Detecting impending recurrence early and injecting before corneal fibrovascular invasion is likely to improve success. A clinical effect typically requires two to four injections, although substantially more have been reported; the authors favor individual consideration. Because antiproliferative activity depends on dose and exposure time, higher doses and repeated treatment may raise complication risk. Injection-only care might avoid surgery and related recurrence or harms, but requires adherence to visits and injections. Long-term safety evidence is insufficient, and optimal injection dose, interval and duration remain undefined. Where 5-FU is used, the authors advise careful selection, caution and vigilant surveillance; patients should be informed of benefits and of possible immediate and delayed risks.

document_sections.heading: 8. Alternatives therapies to 5-fluorouracil
document_sections.content: Corticosteroids, cyclosporine and anti-VEGF agents have also been studied as surgical adjuncts or for impending recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 8.1. Corticosteroids
document_sections.content: Postoperative corticosteroids are routinely used after pterygium surgery. Topical options named are prednisolone, dexamethasone and fluorometholone; subconjunctival agents named are dexamethasone, triamcinolone and hydrocortisone. Inadequate topical postoperative dosing has been suggested as a contributor to higher recurrence. Kheirkhah et al. reported that intraoperative triamcinolone acetonide with bare scleral surgery and mitomycin C did not significantly reduce conjunctival recurrence or inflammation. Topical betamethasone was ineffective for impending recurrence, with 100% progressing onto the cornea. By contrast, postoperative subconjunctival corticosteroid injections appeared more effective against corneal progression in Grade II/III impending recurrence after conjunctival autograft or amniotic membrane graft. In Prabhasawat et al.’s randomized trial, intralesional 5-FU surpassed triamcinolone (87.2% vs. 71.4%), and both exceeded topical steroids alone (48.6%). Clinicians should monitor for steroid-related ocular hypertension.

document_sections.heading: 8.2. Cyclosporine
document_sections.content: Compared with placebo, topical cyclosporine appears to lower recurrence after bare scleral surgery (22% vs. 44% and 20.6% vs. 45.5%), conjunctival rotational flaps (23% vs. 46%), conjunctival autografts (7.5% vs. 17.5%) and limbal-conjunctival autografts. In bilateral disease, Yalcin Tok et al. found 12.9% recurrence in the treated eye versus 45.2% in its control fellow eye. Conversely, Karadag et al. found higher recurrence with cyclosporine plus limbal-conjunctival autograft than with conjunctival autograft alone (26.6% vs. 16.6%). A cited network meta-analysis identified topical cyclosporine as the most successful surgical adjunct to conjunctival autografting for preventing primary-pterygium recurrence. Reported adverse effects include irritation, burning, hyperemia and dellen; graft scarring or scleromalacia is rare.

document_sections.heading: 8.3. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor
document_sections.content: Anti-VEGF agents appear generally well tolerated, but reported effectiveness as surgical adjuncts or treatment of impending recurrence is inconclusive. Subconjunctival ranibizumab (0.5 mg) with conjunctival autograft yielded 33% recurrence at six months. Subconjunctival bevacizumab did not significantly improve recurrence versus placebo with bare scleral surgery (1.25 mg), rotational flaps (1.25, 2.5, 3.75 mg total), or limbal-conjunctival autografts (1.25 mg). In contrast, Nava-Castaneda et al. found corneal recurrence at one year of 0% versus 12.5% (p < 0.04) using bevacizumab (2.5 to 5 mg) with conjunctival autograft versus placebo. One 3.75 mg injection after limbal-conjunctival autograft with limbal fixation suture also lowered recurrence. Topical bevacizumab at 5 mg/ml did not significantly prevent corneal recurrence in studies by Karalezli et al. and Ozgurhan et al.; Motarjemizadeh et al. judged 10 mg/ml effective. For impending recurrence, Fallah et al. observed progression in every case after one 2.5 mg bevacizumab injection. Lekhanont et al. found dose-dependent but temporary vascular regression after one 1.25, 2.5 or 3.75 mg injection, without reduced lesion thickness or size; 78% developed corneal recurrence by three months. Bayar et al., however, reported significantly lower conjunctival vascularity and 95.7% success, with one corneal recurrence, at 12 months after one to three injections. Wu et al. reported regression of limbal-conjunctival neovascularization with topical bevacizumab (25 mg/ml, four times a day, 3 weeks). At 5 mg/ml twice daily for 1 week, Fallah et al. observed only delayed recurrence, with all impending cases eventually extending to the cornea. In true recurrence, Bahar et al. found no significant vascularity reduction after one to two 2.5 mg injections, whereas Nava-Castaneda et al. found three 2.5 mg injections effective against corneal and corneal-conjunctival neovascularization and lesion size. Three studies reported worse recurrence outcomes for bevacizumab than MMC. Bekibele et al. found one 0.5 mg bevacizumab injection comparable to topical intraoperative 5-FU (50 mg/ml, 5 min) with conjunctival autograft. Zhang et al.’s randomized trial found no corneal recurrence after three 2 mg conbercept injections, outperforming 5-FU (5 mg) for impending recurrence. Synergy between 5-FU and bevacizumab has been proposed; Ghoz et al. reported 100% arrest and atrophy in primary disease. The best anti-VEGF dose, schedule, treatment duration and route remain uncertain. Most studies regarded these agents as safe and tolerable, while reporting self-limiting subconjunctival hemorrhage, graft ischemia and graft dehiscence. The review authors also describe a patient whose conjunctival autograft separated, with graft and underlying scleral melting, after preoperative intravitreal aflibercept; Shahin et al. observed a similar complication in one case.

document_sections.heading: 9. Safety and complications of 5-fluorouracil in pterygium
document_sections.content: The complications table summarizes symptoms and ocular findings reported with topical and injected 5-FU. Harms range from minor and transient to sight-threatening. Corneal toxicity is common and is linked to inhibition of epithelial mitosis. Applying 5-FU to bare sclera can cause scleral dellen or thinning (2.5 to 10%). Said et al. proposed that conjunctival coverage protects the antimetabolite-treated sclera. Studies of 5-FU with conjunctival autografts or transpositional flaps reported delayed conjunctival reepithelization (6 to 16%), graft injection (6.5 to 56%), wound separation (7.1 to 32.1%) and graft retraction. The authors previously described conjunctival-graft necrosis and sloughing after pterygium excision with an antimetabolite, attributing it to impairment of the conjunctival and episcleral vascular bed. Symblepharon and cicatricial entropion have also been reported with 5-FU. Rapidly dividing corneal epithelial cells are susceptible to effects on limbal stem cells, as supported by human studies. Reported corneal manifestations include epithelial defects and punctate, filamentary or whorl-like keratopathy. Prabhasawat et al. observed punctate epitheliopathy in 20.5% after two 5 mg injections; three patients had erosions affecting >30% of the cornea, and one eye lost visual acuity. Zhang et al. observed abrasions in 17 of 48 eyes after three 5 mg injections. Stopping 5-FU can reverse some findings, but keratitis, ulceration, melting or perforation can occur, particularly with underlying corneal or ocular-surface disorders. The authors caution against use in patients with previous or current intrinsic corneal disease. Longer corneal exposure during topical administration has been proposed as a cause of more corneal complications, potentially avoidable with targeted injection. Injection studies seem to report lower complication frequencies, although a direct comparison of 25 mg intralesional injection against topical 50 mg/ml for 5 min did not show a significant reduction in the complication proportion. A proposed no-reflux injection method uses a 30-G needle inserted to its hub and cotton-tip pressure over the entry site afterward to keep drug out of the tear film and surrounding surface. Even low-dose treatment has been associated with delayed conjunctival epithelialization (6.4%) and corneal ulceration (6.4%). MMC can cause or be associated with severe ocular complications, and long-term concerns persist despite dose reductions; corneoscleral ulceration and corneal perforation have been reported 18 to 25 years after MMC-assisted excision. Although 5-FU is less potent than MMC, both inhibit proliferation, so similarly serious delayed effects remain a concern. The authors also consider the possibility that pterygium reflects diminished individual DNA-repair capacity. In Australia, around 80% of school-age children have evidence of ocular ultraviolet damage, whereas pterygium prevalence is approximately 7%; this might reflect recovery with time and eye protection. On that conditional reasoning, further suppression of DNA replication could be ill advised, and avoiding 5-FU in those with a family history of pterygium may be preferable.

document_sections.heading: 9.1. Safety profile of 5-fluorouracil in other ocular conditions
document_sections.content: Experience with 5-FU in glaucoma filtration surgery shows frequent punctate epitheliopathy and epithelial defects, generally reversible when injections cease, but occasionally followed by sight-threatening corneal complications. Glaucoma doses are usually higher, reaching up to 105 mg, versus 5 to 20 mg in pterygium. Nonetheless, a glaucoma study using 17.5 to 62.5 mg found 29% corneal epitheliopathy. Another reported a large central epithelial defect, subsequent ulceration and residual scarring after two 10 mg injections. Total intralesional doses used for pterygium overlap that range. For ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), topical 5-FU is usually given as 1% (10 mg/ml) four times daily for one to four weeks followed by a drug-free interval. Reported reactions, usually temporary and reversible, include pain, tearing, light sensitivity, hyperemia, eyelid redness and swelling, and superficial punctate keratitis; epithelial defects occurred in 1 to 8%. Although this 1% regimen has been considered safe, a 2022 case involved sight-threatening bilateral corneoscleral ulceration and unilateral perforation. Epithelial defects appeared at week eight of a biweekly cycle; treatment required repeated amniotic-membrane-ring replacement and eventually a 7.5 mm penetrating keratoplasty. In Sun et al.’s retrospective series of six OSSN cases given perilesional subconjunctival injections (25 mg/ml, 5 to 7.5 mg per dose, mean of 17 injections over 13 weeks), all developed punctate epitheliopathy at four to six weeks, resolving with tear substitutes or bandage contact lenses. No major adverse effects were reported during three years of follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 9.2. Long term safety profile of 5-fluorouracil in pterygium
document_sections.content: Long-term safety evidence for 5-FU in pterygium is scarce. Most published studies have short follow-up, many no longer than six months, and very few exceed 24 months. Although recurrence generally occurs within the first postoperative year, short studies may overlook later drug-related harm. Immediate effects can depend on dose and exposure duration, while delayed concerns persist because antimitotic activity may continue after treatment ends, particularly if ocular-surface stem-cell populations are affected. Antimetabolites used in pterygium and glaucoma have caused or been associated with corneal toxicity, scleral thinning or ulceration, endophthalmitis and calcification many years later. The authors propose extended follow-up in future 5-FU studies to identify potentially harmful delayed effects.

document_sections.heading: 10. Conclusion
document_sections.content: The review finds that 5-FU is inexpensive, available and easy to give, but published evidence shows inadequate prevention of recurrence when it is used before or during surgery. The authors therefore do not recommend it as a pterygium surgical adjuvant. Its recurrence outcomes are inferior to those of emerging surgical techniques, and scleral thinning, corneal toxicity and graft complications are notable concerns. Postoperative intralesional injections, or injections used without surgery, show more promising results for arresting primary, impending recurrent and recurrent disease and improving appearance. Short-term complications with these approaches are generally temporary and reversible, but severe sight-threatening effects remain possible and long-term efficacy and safety evidence is needed. If 5-FU is used, the authors call for caution, patient selection and vigilant long-term monitoring, particularly with repeated exposure. Further injection studies with extended follow-up should determine optimal dose, frequency, duration and safety.
